lesson.title: Invisible Force Around a Wire: Understanding Magnetic Fields
lesson.summary: Every current carrying wire is wrapped in a magnetic field, and coiling that wire concentrates the field into the mechanism behind inductors, motors, and electromagnets.
lesson.body:
In 1820, the Danish physicist Hans Christian Oersted noticed something that seemed impossible at the time: a compass needle near a current carrying wire deflected away from north whenever the current was switched on. Electricity and magnetism, until then treated as entirely separate phenomena, turned out to be two faces of the same underlying physics. Every time charge moves, meaning every time there is current, a magnetic field appears in the space around that motion. You already know current as charge flowing through a conductor, so it is worth internalizing that current never flows alone, it always drags a magnetic field along with it.

Around a long, straight wire, that magnetic field forms neat concentric circles wrapped around the wire's length, like rings stacked around a pole. The direction those circles point follows the right-hand rule: point your right thumb in the direction of conventional current flow, and your curled fingers show the direction the magnetic field circles around the wire. Move farther from the wire and the field spreads out over a larger circle, so its strength weakens with distance, in the same way light spreads out and dims as you move away from a bulb.

The strength of that field is described by B, the magnetic flux density, measured in tesla, and for a long straight wire it follows the formula B equals mu-zero times I, divided by 2 pi times r, where I is the current in amperes, r is the distance from the wire in meters, and mu-zero is the permeability of free space, a fixed constant equal to 4 pi times 10 to the negative seventh tesla meters per ampere. This constant plays a role for magnetic fields similar to the one epsilon-zero plays for electric fields around charge, it sets the baseline strength of the effect in empty space.

Work through an example: a wire carries a steady current of 2 amps, and you want the field strength 5 centimeters, or 0.05 meters, away from it. Plugging into the formula: B equals mu-zero times I, divided by 2 pi times r, which is 4 pi times 10 to the negative seventh, times 2, divided by 2 pi times 0.05. The pi in the numerator and denominator cancel, leaving 4 times 10 to the negative seventh, times 2, divided by 2 times 0.05, which simplifies to 8 times 10 to the negative seventh, divided by 0.1, equal to 8 times 10 to the negative sixth tesla, or 8 microtesla. For comparison, Earth's own magnetic field at the surface is on the order of 50 microtesla, so this single straight wire produces a field roughly a sixth as strong as the planet's, at a distance you could easily reach with your hand.

A single straight wire produces a fairly weak field, but bend that wire into a loop, or better yet wind it into many stacked loops forming a coil, and the fields from every turn add together inside the coil, reinforcing each other into a much stronger, more concentrated field. That reinforcing effect, current through a coiled wire building a concentrated magnetic field, is exactly the physical mechanism behind inductance, and it is why coiled wire, not straight wire, is the basic building block of electromagnets, motor windings, relays, transformers, and every inductor you will work with next.
